## Proof

We interpret an **Operator-homomorphism** $f:M_n(\mathbb C)\to M_n(\mathbb C)$ as a unital $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism: $f$ is $\mathbb C$-linear, $f(AB)=f(A)f(B)$, and $f(I)=I$.

### Step 1. $f$ is an automorphism.

$M_n(\mathbb C)$ is a simple algebra: its only two-sided ideals are $\{0\}$ and itself. The kernel $\ker f$ is a two-sided ideal. Since $f(I)=I\neq 0$, $f$ is not the zero map, so $\ker f\neq M_n(\mathbb C)$; hence $\ker f=\{0\}$ and $f$ is injective. As a linear endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space, injectivity implies bijectivity. Thus $f$ is an algebra automorphism.

### Step 2. Matrix units and their images.

Let $E_{ij}\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be the standard matrix units, satisfying
$$E_{ij}E_{kl}=\delta_{jk}E_{il},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n E_{ii}=I.$$
Set $F_{ij}:=f(E_{ij})$. Since $f$ is a unital homomorphism,
$$F_{ij}F_{kl}=\delta_{jk}F_{il},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n F_{ii}=I,\qquad F_{ij}\neq 0.$$

### Step 3. Each $F_{ii}$ has rank $1$.

From $F_{ii}^2=F_{ii}$, each $F_{ii}$ is an idempotent. From $F_{ii}F_{jj}=0$ for $i\neq j$ and $\sum F_{ii}=I$, the $F_{ii}$ are mutually orthogonal idempotents summing to $I$.

The relations $F_{ij}F_{ji}=F_{ii}$ and $F_{ji}F_{ij}=F_{jj}$ show that $F_{ij}$ (resp. $F_{ji}$) restricts to an isomorphism between $\operatorname{im}F_{jj}$ and $\operatorname{im}F_{ii}$. Hence all $\operatorname{im}F_{ii}$ have the same dimension $r\ge 1$ (nonzero since $F_{ii}\neq 0$). Then
$$n=\operatorname{rank}(I)=\operatorname{rank}\Big(\sum_i F_{ii}\Big)=\sum_i \operatorname{rank}(F_{ii})=nr,$$
so $r=1$. Every $F_{ii}$ is a rank-$1$ idempotent.

### Step 4. Constructing a basis.

Pick any nonzero $v_1\in\operatorname{im}F_{11}$, and define
$$v_i:=F_{i1}v_1,\qquad i=1,\dots,n.$$
Then $F_{ii}v_i=F_{ii}F_{i1}v_1=F_{i1}v_1=v_i$, so $v_i\in\operatorname{im}F_{ii}$. Moreover $v_i\neq 0$, since $F_{1i}v_i=F_{1i}F_{i1}v_1=F_{11}v_1=v_1\neq 0$.

**Linear independence.** If $\sum_i c_i v_i=0$, applying $F_{jj}$ gives $c_j v_j=0$, hence $c_j=0$. So $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb C^n$.

### Step 5. $f$ is inner.

Let $P$ be the invertible matrix with columns $v_1,\dots,v_n$, i.e. $Pe_i=v_i$. For every $i,j,k$,
$$F_{ij}v_k=F_{ij}F_{k1}v_1=\delta_{jk}F_{i1}v_1=\delta_{jk}v_i.$$
On the other hand,
$$PE_{ij}P^{-1}v_k=PE_{ij}e_k=P(\delta_{jk}e_i)=\delta_{jk}v_i.$$
Thus $F_{ij}$ and $PE_{ij}P^{-1}$ agree on the basis $\{v_k\}$, so
$$f(E_{ij})=F_{ij}=PE_{ij}P^{-1}\qquad\text{for all }i,j.$$
Since $\{E_{ij}\}$ is a $\mathbb C$-basis of $M_n(\mathbb C)$ and $f$ is linear, linearity extends this to all of $M_n(\mathbb C)$:
$$f(A)=PAP^{-1}\qquad\text{for all }A\in M_n(\mathbb C).$$
Setting $Q:=P^{-1}$ (which is invertible), we obtain
$$\boxed{\,f(A)=Q^{-1}AQ\,}$$
for some invertible $Q\in M_n(\mathbb C)$.

### Step 6. Converse.

Conversely, for any invertible $P$, the map $A\mapsto P^{-1}AP$ is clearly a unital $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism (hence an Operator-homomorphism). This completes the characterization.

---

Therefore every Operator-homomorphism $f:M_n(\mathbb C)\to M_n(\mathbb C)$ is of the form $f(A)=P^{-1}AP$ for some invertible $P\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, and conversely. $\blacksquare$
